content.thinking:
I'm planning to write the whole file in one careful pass without testing, designing an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike with bold clean shapes, gunmetal and white panels, and a single orange accent with glow lights. I'm sketching real-world proportions—roughly 2.5m long, 1.1m tall, apehanger handlebars up to 1.3m—with the bike facing forward along +Z.

Now I'm working out wheel sizes and axle positions for front and rear, then planning the joint hierarchy: a root frame with steering, front/rear wheel hinges, swingarm, and kickstand joints. I'm also figuring out how to orient the cylinder and torus geometries so wheels and tires align correctly along the X axis, picking specific radius and tube values for the front and rear tires so they sit properly on the ground.

Now I'm computing the fork's steering joint geometry for the chopper's raked front end—setting a steep 40° rake angle with a direction vector, then working out the fork length and head tube position needed to reach the front axle at the correct height and offset.

I'm also laying out the frame structure: positioning the front axle, confirming a ~2m wheelbase, and planning the hardtail frame tubes connecting the head tube, seat area, engine mount, and rear dropouts using rod elements with explicit bone assignments.

Now I'm shaping the fuel tank using lofted stations along the frame to create a teardrop profile, defining width and height at several points from front to back.

Writing paint gradient logic...

For the seat I'm planning a thin dark leather loft positioned near the rear, possibly with ribbed stitching created by a sine-based darkening pattern along the z-axis. For the engine, I'm sketching a V-twin with a crankcase box and two angled cylinders in the side profile, topped with stacked disc cooling fins.

Setting cylinder angles and positions...

I'm planning the exhaust pipes sweeping from the heads back along the right side with a curved, flared path, keeping colors flat and limited to around 20 for the metallic parts.

No conflicts with the swingarm or fender, so I'll add a heat shield as a perforated box section with a few small clamp rings. For the left side, I'm planning a primary drive cover disc at the engine and a thin flat belt rod connecting the engine sprocket to the rear sprocket using a box-section rod.

Now I'm moving to the front end: fork tubes, triple tree plates, a headlight lathe shape with glow lens, speedo, and apehanger handlebars built from a catmull sweep rising from the clamps up through the steer joint at the head, curving outward as real apes do.

I'm deciding peak height around 1.32 for a realistic chopper look, then adding grips, small brake levers, and mirror stems with an extruded oval lens. All these parts attach to the steer bone so the front fender, built as an arc sweep over the front wheel following the fork, moves correctly with the steering.

Writing fender sweep path...

The fork and wheel are both children of the steer bone so they rotate together correctly. Now I'm defining the fork as two sliders: chrome upper stanchions and darker lower legs, setting up a direction vector and a helper function to position points along that line from the head tube down to the axle.

Still writing fork geometry...

Designing wheel geometry...

I'll switch to using thin cylinders aimed between points instead, since that avoids the orientation ambiguity—8 spokes per wheel across both wheels, keeping total part count well under budget. Then I'll move on to the rear hardtail triangle, adding seat stay and chain stay rods running from the rear axle up to the seat post.

For finishing touches, I'll add a rear fender arcing over the wheel, a small red glow box for the tail light, and a fictional license plate with made-up characters so there's no real branding. I'll skip springer forks, and add forward control foot pegs as small cylinders mounted near the frame.

I also need a kickstand hinged to the frame, folded back along the chain stay so it doesn't touch the ground, and I'm double-checking that the lowest points of the bike—the tire contact patches—sit right at y=0 by matching axle heights to wheel plus tire radius for both front and rear.

Working through the torus tire dimensions, I realize the scale only affects the tube width (Z-axis), not the outer radius, so I'm adjusting tube and radius values to get a fat rear tire (~0.38 outer radius) and a slightly narrower front, aiming for realistic chopper proportions.

Rather than UV-painting tread details, I'm opting to build a tread ring by generating small box geometries placed radially around the tire using matrix transforms, then merging them into one geometry per wheel for the tread blocks.

I'm working out the wheel geometry further: an orange accent ring on the torus, rim lip radius, and spokes running from the hub out to the rim. I'm also considering adding a flat disc behind the spokes to mimic a mag-wheel look with five broad spokes.

For the rear wheel I'm adjusting the torus radius and tube thickness to give a fatter tire with a slightly narrower rim, then setting up a reusable wheel-building helper function that takes center, radius, tube, and width parameters. Now I'm positioning the headlight on the front fork so it stays attached and turns with the steering, calculating its y and z offsets based on the fork angle.

Lathing headlight housing shape...

Adding the rim torus and glowing lens disc for the headlight, then sketching a small speedometer disc near the handlebar clamp. I'm settling on one accent color—orange—for the glow highlights across headlight, taillight, and other emissive parts.

Now I'm defining the overall color palette: orange and darker orange for accents, cream/white and navy/dark for the body, gunmetal and steel tones for metal parts, chrome, black, rubber, and leather browns for the remaining surfaces.

I'm planning engine paint using a mottled gunmetal-to-steel texture to simulate worn metal, then thinking through which imports I'll actually need—THREE.js utilities, path and texture helpers, glow and paint tools, and geometry merging—while being careful to avoid unused imports that could trigger type errors.

Setting up the builder with named joints for the chopper's frame and head positioning...

Still defining joints...

Still defining geometry helpers...

I'm thinking through the color scheme for an Overwatch-style bike: dark gunmetal frame with orange accents, orange/white tank, orange fenders, and dark wheels with orange rims. Now I'm mapping out the frame tube geometry, starting with the head tube following the fork axis.

Plotting the frame rails...

Still adding frame geometry... I'm also adding seat stays, rear axle plates, and engine mount boxes, then placing the rear axle cylinder. I realize the rail position at x±0.1 would clip through the fat rear tire, so I need to adjust that.

I'm widening the rails and seat stays outward to x≈0.15-0.165 to clear the tire, narrowing the fender half-width to about 0.14 so it still fits beside the seat stays without overlapping, then moving on to position the tank on top of the top tube.

I'm adding a small chrome gas cap near the tank top, then designing an abstract decal (avoiding any real logos) — a bolt-stripe or flame-swoosh shape applied to the tank sides as a surface texture rather than a flat sticker.

Now I'm working out mirroring so the swoosh decal reads correctly from both sides, since the viewer's left-right orientation flips depending on which flank is facing the camera.

I'll avoid text on the decals entirely to sidestep rendering risk, saving any text for just the license plate itself. For the seat, I'm sketching a loft profile with stations running from near the top tube down to above the rear fender, checking clearances against the top tube radius and rear wheel position.

Checking the fender geometry against the axle position confirms the seat sits clear above it. For the seat material I'm adding a leather paint function with periodic rib striping based on sine waves along the z-axis plus a center stitch strip, and I'll add a seat pan/bracket box underneath to support it.

Shaping the rear fender sweep...

Working out the tail light position and sizing, then the plate bracket hanging below it, plus noting I still need the exhaust heat shield and the engine crankcase geometry next.

Building crankcase shape...

Now I'm placing the left primary cover as a cylinder with an orange bolt ring, and adding a chrome air cleaner housing lathed on the carburetor side between the cylinders.

Checking clearance against the exhaust pipe path confirms no collision there. For the cylinders themselves, I'm positioning each barrel along its V-angle direction from the crank pivot with cast iron coloring, then adding seven cooling fin discs spaced along the barrel length.

Now I'm shaping the heads at the top of each barrel using boxes for rocker covers painted orange, plus routing the exhaust pipes starting from the front cylinder's port location, curving down and outward through several waypoints toward the rear.

I'm checking that the pipe routing doesn't collide with footpeg placement -- adjusting the pegs forward near z=0.5 while keeping the pipes lower and clear, then moving on to plan the rear cylinder's exhaust path.

Still routing exhaust geometry...

Still figuring out clamp orientation...

Now I'm planning bone assignment for path segments, defaulting to the nearest joint when the path has no inherent bones, with torus detail parameters for the clamp geometry. Moving on to foot controls—pegs, shifter rod, and brake pedal placement—before tackling handlebars and throttle geometry.

For the handlebars, I'm positioning the riser clamp at the top of the triple tree and sweeping a curve up and back toward the rider to form apehanger-style bars, checking that grip height and reach stay proportional to the seat position and overall bike height.

Setting the grip to span z from 0.2 to 0.06, centered with length 0.14, and placing the gripL hinge joint there with a downward direction tied to the grip bone. Mirroring to the right side as gripR, then moving on to the clutch lever geometry on the left side.

Working out the lever bracket and rod geometry with its hinge joint and radius, capped with a small ball end, then mirroring the mirror stems and ellipsoid head shapes on both sides, oriented thin along the z-axis to face rearward.

For color, I'm giving the mirror a chrome rim with a steel-blue glass face set slightly in front, offset toward the rider. Then I'm working through fork details: chrome upper stanchions with their radius and length, gun-metal lowers with axle ends and steel cap bolts, plus the triple tree boxes connecting them.

I'm adjusting the triple tree box dimensions to align with the fork's direction, placing two trees along the fork, and adding small orange-painted ring accents on the mid fork segment. Then I'm figuring out the fender stay rods, calculating the fender's forward-angled position and where the support rods attach between the fender and fork.

Checking tire clearance along that stay rod path, I'm nudging the x-offset outward to 0.085 so the thin rod stays clear of the tire radius. I'm also catching a potential conflict where the fork lower's inner edge sits inside the scaled tire's half-width, so I need to adjust the fork x-position outward too.

Rethinking the geometry: the tire only exists in a radius band from the axle, and the fork leg crosses that band near the axle, so I'm checking clearance there and settling on fork offset ±0.09 with slightly thinner stanchions, widening the fork trees to 0.22 and giving the hub axle enough length. Rear wheel has no such conflict. For the front brake disc, I'm placing it at a radius smaller than the inner rim so it tucks inside the tire profile without interference, then moving on to actually modeling the disc shape.

For the disc I'm using a thin textured cylinder to fake brake-rotor holes, offset slightly on each side of center to simulate double-sided visibility, then positioning an orange caliper box straddling the fork leg just behind the axle. I'm also sizing the front hub as a steel cylinder with an axle nut, and planning a larger rear hub with a belt pulley/sprocket disc mounted outboard of the tire so its teeth clear the tire's inner rim radius.

Now I'm repositioning the rear pulley and axle plates further out along x to avoid overlapping, adding a rear disc brake and caliper on the opposite side, and starting to lay out the belt path between the primary engine pulley and the rear pulley based on their coordinates.

Good, confirmed belt width runs along X with the thin dimension vertical along Y, which matches the YZ-plane loop geometry. Now I'm considering the chain guard cover, noting this is a hardtail so no rear shock but a seat spring instead, and positioning an oil tank cylinder under the seat.

I'm placing the oil tank cylinder and battery box coordinates, adjusting the tank radius and height along with rail and top tube positions, then moving on to engine plate bolt details and the spark plug wire curves running from the head to the coil.

Now I'm sketching a chrome sissy bar behind the seat as a smooth curved sweep forming a symmetric arc, joining both sides at a top bar with a continuous catmull path, then adding a small leather back pad detail.

I'm positioning that pad behind the sissy bar with a slight backward tilt, and figuring out the rotation math so the top leans toward negative z. Then I'm checking how the sissy bar relates to the fender mount position at various heights.

Now I'm working out the headlight bracket placement, tracing rods from the fork stanchions up to the headlight housing. I notice the headlight's radius causes it to overlap with the fork legs at the current position, so I'm adjusting the headlight center forward in z to clear that collision.

I decide to skip a complex visor shape and instead add a simple thin orange torus ring around the headlight lens for styling, then move on to placing a small tilted cylinder for the speedometer near the handlebars.

For the speedo, I'm giving it a rim housing and a glowing face angled toward the rider, checking whether its position might overlap with the front edge of the tank.

I nudge the tank's starting station back slightly to avoid clashing with the cap, then move on to placing the tank's side decals, positioning them relative to the tank's width so they project correctly onto the curved surface.

Next I work out the kickstand geometry — a rod running from its pivot joint down to the foot pad, stowed along the frame with a small spring detail. Then I lay out the brake/clutch cables as curved sweeps from the handlebar levers down to the head, using smooth control points for a natural bend, and plan to mirror this setup for both sides.

I route the throttle cable from the grip down to the carb cleaner area as a longer bone-following curve. Then I plan which parts should get a glow effect — headlight lens, speedo face, taillight, exhaust ring, primary cover accent — and start designing an SVG texture for the brake disc with concentric rings and a ventilation hole pattern generated in a loop.

Writing SVG decal paths...

I'll skip the wheel face and move to a license plate design with "CH-07" text centered in navy on a white background with a navy border. I'm also considering seat stitching details next.

Fender stripe is handled by paint. For tires, I'm writing a function that generates tread blocks by creating rotated box geometries around the wheel's circumference and merging them into one mesh, using quaternions for angular placement so each block sits radially and tangentially correct. I'm also planning a torus shape for the tread crown at the wheel's equator.

Now I'm working out shoulder blocks positioned at angled offsets from the crown—placing them at roughly ±50° around the tube cross-section so they sit on the sidewall curve, computing their radial and lateral positions using sine and cosine of that angle, and figuring out how to tilt their rotation to match the curvature there.

Writing wheel builder function...

Working out the sidewall accent stripe placement...

Computing sidewall ring placement...

Then for the rim, I'm using a torus with steel coloring plus a thin orange accent ring, and setting up spoke positions around the hub using angular offsets for each spoke index.

Figuring out box dimensions confirms default roll aligns width along world X, so a thin flat box works for each spoke. I'm planning five front spokes and six rear ones with a rim accent, plus an orange hubcap disc and center cap cylinder for the wheel detail.

I'm adding an orange accent torus inside the rim, scaled to fit, while skipping the valve stem detail. Now I'm moving on to composing the full wheel assembly and starting the handlebar group.

Still planning grip and foot control details, deciding to skip the number plate and side panel additions for simplicity, and starting to define the color palette constants before writing the final code.

Finishing the color palette and starting a tank paint helper function that shades colors based on position...

Writing shading logic...

Skipping orange piping on seat sides for now. I'm setting up metal mottling for gunmetal surfaces, a lit engine paint blending steel and gunmetal tones, and an orange lit paint for the primary cover, plus a `lit` helper function. Now I'm starting the cylinder geometry function with parameters for position, direction, radii, length, and bone attachment.

Still writing part helpers... I'm sorting out the right Fill/ColorInput type imports from context and paint modules, orienting cylinders along the x-axis, and building a bolt helper plus a bolt-ring function that arranges bolts in a circle around a given axis.

Now I'm structuring the main build function—starting the chassis joint and setting up the overall builder config before laying out the rest of the motorbike's parts in order.

For the fork geometry, I'm computing the head position and fork direction vector, then deriving the axle position along the fork line so the tire sits correctly against the ground with minimal sinkage.

Now I'm writing the wheel builder function, defining the torus for the tire tread and setting up the geometry arrays for the tread blocks and rim details...

Placing each box segment with calculated position and rotation...

Writing spoke geometry loop...

I'll skip the tapered segment approach for now and add an orange inner ring plus hub detail. Then I'll move on to building the exhaust using swept geometry.

Adding exhaust pipe sweep...

Adding engine fins, head block, and rocker cover geometry...

I'm skipping the pushrod detail and adding a small lateral spark plug cylinder with ceramic coloring, then attaching the engine rigidly to the chassis bone. I'll leave carb and transmission details minimal, and plan to build frame tubes using a sweep function along a spline with circular cross-section.

I'm working out a helper `tube` function that wraps `sweep` with a catmull spline, radius, color, and bone, defining the radius type as either a fixed number or a function of t. For straight two-point rods I'll just use a simpler `rod` helper instead of forcing catmull through only two points.

Now I'm building the steering mechanism parts: bars using the tube helper with a steer bone, then symmetric grip and lever joints (gripL/gripR, leverL/leverR) positioned and oriented off the steer parent for each side. After that I'm adding the throttle cable and the brake master cylinder on the right bar with the clutch on the left.

Now I'm working out the fork lowers with orange sleeves and the front axle cylinder, then computing the front fender's path using trig to position points around the axle radius while checking clearance against the fork stanchions.

I'm resolving an overlap between the fender and fork legs by widening the fork offset to 0.105 and setting the fender half-width to 0.07, verifying this still clears the tire width and leaves enough gap between the fender and tire outer radius.

Still computing fender stay geometry...

Setting fender half-width around 0.145 and checking that rear stays clear the fender region, confirming the seat stay path stays outside the 0.45 radius near the axle and only approaches it near the dropout end.

I'll just adjust the fender radius and stay positions outward to avoid overlap, then lock in placements: fender rx 0.135, stays at x=±0.175, axle plate at x=±0.175, pulley at x=0.215, and axle length to ±0.26. The build order for frame parts doesn't matter, so I'll move on to the seat stays, and set the rear brake disc at x=-0.19.

Next I'm sizing the rear brake disc and caliper, then defining the belt pulley geometry with flanges, foot pegs, and finally assembling the complete file including a tail light, rear license plate with texture and backing plate, and a mounting bracket computed from the fender's end angle.

For the tail light, I'm placing a small glowing red box near the fender's underside, roughly adjacent to the plate bracket, then moving on to the sissy bar pad and exhaust tip details before writing the file. I'm also working out the shifter and brake lever positions as rods running from the footpeg area to pedal points on each side, with the pegs themselves as short cylinders extending outward from the frame.

Now I'm double-checking color definitions, making sure the mottle paint function for the engine crankcase uses nested color inputs correctly, and verifying that all imports (mix, paint, smoothstep, mottle) are actually used. I'm also confirming the glow helper works on parts with flat color strings before moving into SVG generation.

Writing decal placement...

Now I'm refining the tank's loft station coordinates, adjusting the z-positions, widths, heights, and y-offsets so the tank bottom aligns properly against the frame's top tube near z=0.05.

I'm plotting the top tube path points and checking that the fuel cap sits correctly on the tank top with a chrome cylinder plus orange inner detail, then positioning the speedometer near the tank nose on the dash riser.

Adding bolt ring helper function...

I'm tallying the color palette to stay under the 64-color limit, checking off flat part colors and the glow tone for the exhaust ring.
